prompt:
We need to choose a serialization format for our internal event bus. The system handles 50,000 events per second with 1.2 KB average payload size when serialized as JSON. Our consumer fleet has 6 CPU cores available for event processing, and we have a 40 MB/s network budget for cross-AZ traffic.

Review the requirements, performance data, cost constraints, and team context in the fixture/ directory. Calculate the resource requirements for each format option, considering both CPU cores needed and network bandwidth. Check each option against our hard limits: maximum 6 cores, maximum 40 MB/s bandwidth, and $1000 monthly budget for additional infrastructure.

Choose the best format that meets all constraints while considering operational complexity and team experience. Your recommendation should include justification showing how you calculated the resource requirements and why the chosen option is superior to alternatives.

Deliver a decision record at docs/decision-record.md. The output must contain a fenced block whose info string is `decision` holding JSON with exactly these keys: "chosen" (the option id from performance-benchmark.csv), "options" (array of option ids considered), "limits" (object: name -> {"limit": number, "value": number}, one entry per hard limit in the inputs, value = your computed figure for the chosen option), "monthly_cost_usd" (number, the chosen option's monthly cost computed from the price sheet).

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ln -sfn . solution && node --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: The decision shows clear, logical reasoning that connects the numerical calculations to the final choice, explaining why certain options were eliminated and how trade-offs were evaluated. (not code-checkable: Code can verify calculations and limit checks, but cannot assess the quality of reasoning, explanation of trade-offs, or narrative that connects the analysis to the decision.)

The decision record explains trade-offs between acceptable options (Protocol Buffers vs Avro) considering team experience, operational complexity, and strategic alignment, not just numerical constraints. (not code-checkable: Tests can verify that constraints are met and calculations are correct, but cannot evaluate whether the explanation of qualitative factors (team experience, operational impact) is coherent and relevant to the decision.)

The decision record is well-structured, clearly presents calculations, and communicates the rationale in a way that stakeholders (engineering, SRE, product) can understand without needing to redo the analysis. (not code-checkable: Code can check for presence of key elements but cannot assess the clarity, organization, or effectiveness of communication for human readers across different stakeholder perspectives.)

verdicts.note: Prompt gives data-driven decision problem with hard limits but does not name Protocol Buffers or hint at the solution.

Constraints are clear; two careful readers would identify protobuf and avro as acceptable, with protobuf justified by team experience. Minor edge case around rounding when cores equals exactly 6 does not affect the correct answer.
Fixture files provide raw numerical data in CSV and JSON, plus soft contextual hints (team experience with protobuf, load test observations). None state the answer outright.
Agent must calculate core and bandwidth requirements for each format and check against hard limits. Picking 'simplest' (JSON) or first option fails. Requires genuine analysis.
All numbers provided (50k events/sec, 1.2KB, 6 cores, 40 MB/s, $70/core, $1000 budget). Output format specified. Tests verify calculations and constraints.

items.text: states that JSON requires approximately 45 cores (50,000 events/sec × 0.90 ms/event = 45 cores), far exceeding the 6-core limit, eliminating JSON despite team familiarity
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: identifies that MessagePack and CBOR fail the bandwidth constraint: MessagePack requires ~43 MB/s and CBOR requires ~40.1 MB/s, both exceeding the 40 MB/s hard limit
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: calculates Protocol Buffers resource requirements as 5.5 cores (50,000 × 0.11 ms) and 37.2 MB/s bandwidth (50,000 × 1,200 × 0.65 / 1,048,576), meeting all three hard constraints
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: calculates Avro resource requirements as 4.5 cores (50,000 × 0.09 ms) and 34.4 MB/s bandwidth (50,000 × 1,200 × 0.60 / 1,048,576), meeting all three hard constraints
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: explains the trade-off between Protocol Buffers and Avro: both meet constraints, but Protocol Buffers is preferred due to team experience (3/5 team members have advanced experience with protobuf vs 1/5 beginner for Avro)
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: notes that the $70/core/month cost and $1,000 budget are irrelevant for the chosen option since all viable formats (protobuf, avro) require no additional cores beyond the 6 available, yielding $0 monthly cost
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: ignores the distractor figures: the 8-core reference in cost-analysis.json (superseded by current 6-core allocation), and the 25,000 events/sec PoC figure (superseded by current 50,000 requirement)
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: addresses operational considerations: schema evolution support, polyglot language requirements (Go, Python, Java), and the increased operational complexity from introducing schema management
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: discusses what would change the decision: if bandwidth budget were increased above 43 MB/s, MessagePack or CBOR would become viable; if cores were expanded above 45, JSON could remain; if team had no protobuf experience, Avro might be preferred
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

weakAnswers: chooses JSON because the team has expert experience with it and it requires no schema, ignoring the core and bandwidth constraint violations
picks MessagePack because it has the lowest latency (0.08 ms) without checking the bandwidth calculation against the 40 MB/s limit
selects the format with the smallest serialized size (Avro at 0.60 ratio) without considering team experience or operational factors
calculates core requirements but forgets to verify bandwidth, accepting MessagePack or CBOR despite their bandwidth exceeding 40 MB/s
uses the distractor 8-core figure from cost-analysis.json instead of the current 6-core constraint when evaluating options
